about: A hawker and his one dish

lines.text: Mr Goh has stood behind the same stall at the hawker centre for
forty years. He sells only one dish, a bowl of fishball noodles, or
lines.note: Connector: he is adding a second fact, so it is 'and', not 'or'.

lines.text: he has never changed the recipe. His day begins long before sunrise, when
he mixes fresh fish paste by hand and shape every ball himself. By
lines.note: Agreement: 'he mixes … and shapes' — both verbs go with 'he'.

lines.text: six o’clock, a queue has usually formed at front of the stall.
lines.note: Preposition: the phrase is 'in front of'.

lines.text: Many of his customers first came as children and now bring its own
lines.note: Pronoun: 'customers' are people and plural, so it is 'their'.

lines.text: children along. Mr Goh remembers most of their orders without being told. He
could have retire years ago, for his three sons all earn good salaries.
lines.note: Verb form: after 'could have' it is 'retired'.

lines.text: However, he insists that cooking is good for him than resting at home.
Nobody in the family has yet agreed to take over a stall, so
lines.note: Article: it is his own stall, already mentioned, so it is 'the stall'.

lines.text: he worries that the taste will disappear when he finally stopped working. For
lines.note: Tense: this is about the future, so it is 'when he finally stops'.

lines.text: now, though, the queue is as long as it has ever been.
